reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferation of the plantar aponeurosis, presenting as one or more firm, slowly enlarging nodules in the medial or central band of the arch

Nodules are typically fixed to the fascia but mobile relative to overlying skin, and are often bilateral; unlike Dupuytren disease they seldom produce fixed toe contractures because the digital extensions of the fascia are less involved
It forms part of the superficial fibromatosis or fibromatosis diathesis, so associations with Dupuytren contracture of the hand, Peyronie disease and Garrod knuckle pads should be sought
Reported associations include diabetes, chronic alcohol use, chronic liver disease, epilepsy and long-term anticonvulsant therapy

MRI is characteristic, showing an infiltrative fascial lesion that is typically low to intermediate in signal on both T1 and T2 owing to its dense collagen content, which helps distinguish it from a sarcoma
Histology shows bland spindled myofibroblasts within dense collagen without atypia, distinguishing it from fibrosarcoma and other malignant soft-tissue tumours
First-line treatment is non-operative with soft accommodative orthoses and padding to offload the nodule; surgery is reserved for disabling disease and carries a high recurrence rate
Recurrence is substantially lower after wide or complete plantar fasciectomy than after simple local nodule excision, at the cost of greater morbidity
reference.pathophysiology: Plantar fibromatosis is a locally infiltrative but biologically benign proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts within the plantar aponeurosis, most often the medial band. Disordered wound-healing-type signalling with excess transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor drives myofibroblast proliferation and deposition of dense type III and type I collagen, producing the palpable nodules. Repetitive microtrauma, a genetic predisposition shared with other superficial fibromatoses, and metabolic factors such as diabetes and alcohol are thought to contribute. Progression through cellular proliferative, involutional and residual collagenous phases parallels the pattern seen in Dupuytren disease, though contracture of the toes is far less common because the vertical and digital fascial extensions are relatively spared.
additionalDifferentials: Plantar fibroma versus a soft-tissue sarcoma such as synovial sarcoma or fibrosarcoma
Plantar fascial rupture or chronic plantar fasciitis with a fibrotic nodule
Ganglion or epidermal inclusion cyst of the sole
Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath or fibrolipoma
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the foot to characterise fascial origin, collagen-rich signal and extent before intervention
Ultrasound demonstrating a hypoechoic fusiform nodule contiguous with the plantar fascia
Examination of the hands and, where relevant, the penis for associated superficial fibromatoses
Core or excisional biopsy with histology when malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging
Screening for associated conditions such as diabetes and chronic liver disease
Baseline photographic and clinical mapping of nodule number and size for monitoring
redFlags: Rapid growth, size beyond a few centimetres, or a deep and poorly defined mass suggesting sarcoma
High T2 signal, marked enhancement or bony involvement on imaging atypical for benign fibromatosis
Skin ulceration, fixation or neurovascular compromise
reference.prognosis: Plantar fibromatosis is benign and does not metastasise, but it is prone to local recurrence, and postoperative recurrence is common after limited excision; symptoms are often controlled long term with orthoses, with surgery reserved for refractory disabling disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking an aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma for a benign fibroma and performing an unplanned marginal excision
Undertaking simple nodule excision and underestimating the high recurrence risk compared with wider fasciectomy
Damaging plantar nerves or creating a painful plantar scar and contracture during surgery
Attributing arch pain solely to plantar fasciitis and missing an underlying fibromatosis nodule
